An engrossing, entertaining look at the distinction between fact and fiction.
It’s what you call a good time.

In essence, "The Lifespan of a Fact," which opened Thursday night at Studio 54, is a fun debate play, commercial catnip for the brain, the kind of old-school, celebrity-friendly show you can argue about over late-night pasta without anyone's face landing in the sauce.

The spry humor, rippling tension and provocative reflections of this ingenious adaptation of the sui generis book of the same name will by no means speak exclusively to those of us who make our livings as members of the fourth estate.
An intriguing premise and a confident assemblage of ideas fall apart onstage despite a trio of strong performances

“A new based-on-reality play starring a totally-committed triumvirate...poses some big questions about small truths. Certainly the top-grade quality of the cast has us hoping for answers, or at least a rousing good yarn. There’s a little disappointed on both fronts...
This clever and nuanced play is less in thrall to the romance of longform narrative as it is in the grinding business of getting things right, in telling as close to the truth as one can.

And while the work strives to be even-handed, it's clear the playwrights are more sympathetic to Jim's side of the debate. Daniel Radcliffe plays the unrelenting noodge to perfection. And when the two go at it, Bobby Cannavale's arch sense of entitlement as John makes for a most compelling dynamic.

The ending lands with surprising emotional resonance too, though the impact of its final moments mostly serves to remind theatergoers that the rest of Lifespan could have used another, altruistic kind of fiction: more plot — and true emotional detail — than its bare facts can provide.

What's most impressive about this stage version, written by Jeremy Kareken, David Murrell and Gordon Farrell and directed by Leigh Silverman ("Violet"), is that it transforms something potentially insider-ish and wonky into a surprisingly funny and urgent drama.
While setting out with excellent intention, the play runs off the rails about half way in.
The verbal volleys can be fun, but some of the action seems silly and contrived: When Jim somehow ends up hiding in a closet, it’s like something out of a “Three’s Company” episode.

While the production (directed by Leigh Silverman, “Violet”) is lively and centered on three great actors fighting it out, the play itself is rather thin (little more than the back-and-forth dialogue on which it is based) and the characters are all one-dimensional.
The play The Lifespan of a Fact is an amusing evening at the theater.
But it makes for a weirdly compelling 95 minutes.
Beyond the nonsense that “The Lifespan of a Fact” makes of journalism, there is the little dramatic problem that none of the three characters grows or develops in the course of 90 minutes.
This play raises an important question, but hardly scratches the surface about western media‘s fake news.

cn.t: Critics find this journalism ethics debate timely and well-acted by Radcliffe, Jones, and Cannavale, but many feel the provocative premise doesn't fully develop into a satisfying drama, resulting in mixed-positive reviews.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
